source_evidence.observation: The one-dimensional exact transform is the unnormalized complex Fourier transform y(j) = sum from k = 0 to N - 1 of exp(i 2 pi j k/N)x(k), with j = 0,...,N - 1 and i = sqrt(-1); the paper defines RMS by averaging squared complex magnitudes.

The Fourier matrix is factored into permutation matrices, block Fourier matrices of orders N_r, and diagonal twiddle-factor matrices for an order N = product of the N_r. The paper states that the factorization covers both Cooley-Tukey and Sande-Tukey algorithms, with different diagonal matrices.

For floating-point operands a and b, the paper models addition by fl(a+b) = a(1+theta epsilon)+b(1+theta epsilon) and multiplication by fl(ab) = ab(1+theta epsilon), where each occurrence of theta may differ and always lies between -1 and 1.

The paper introduces gamma >= 0 with fl(sin(fl(a))) = sin(a)+gamma theta epsilon and fl(cos(fl(a))) = cos(a)+gamma theta epsilon. Gamma depends on the computation of the trigonometric values and their arguments for a given transform order, but not on the input data.

For a one-dimensional mixed-radix FFT of order N = product from r = 1 to M of N_r, Theorem 1 defines K(N,gamma) = sum from r = 1 to M of alpha(N_r) + (M-1)(3+2 gamma), where alpha(2) = sqrt(2), alpha(4) = 5, and alpha(n) = 2 sqrt(n)(n+gamma) otherwise.
The proof expands products of factors 1+theta epsilon and says that O(epsilon^2) collects terms of order epsilon^2.
The exact multidimensional transform is Y(t_1,...,t_m) = sum over s_1,...,s_m of e(s_1t_1/N_1 + ... + s_mt_m/N_m)X(s_1,...,s_m), with s_l,t_l = 0,...,N_l-1 for every l = 1,...,m.

The paper defines E(t_1,...,t_m) = fl(Y(t_1,...,t_m))-Y(t_1,...,t_m), its RMS over all N_1...N_m output coordinates, and its maximum magnitude. Theorem 2 gives both a relative RMS bound and a maximum-error-to-output-RMS bound.

source_evidence.anchor: nested computation, telescoping decomposition, and equations (4.2)-(4.4)
source_evidence.observation: With Z_0 = Y, Z_m = X, and Z_{l-1} = T_l Z_l, the computed result is written as fl(T_1 fl(T_2 ... fl(T_m X)...)). The proof decomposes its error into propagated local transform errors and states the local estimate [fl(Z_{l-1})-Z_{l-1}]_RMS/[Z_l]_RMS <= epsilon sqrt(N_l)K(N_l,gamma)+O(epsilon^2) and the exact scaling [Z_{l-1}]_RMS = sqrt(N_l)[Z_l]_RMS.

source_evidence.anchor: completion of the proof of Theorem 2(a)
source_evidence.observation: The propagated local bounds produce an absolute RMS bound whose l-th first-order term is epsilon sqrt(N_1...N_l)K(N_l,gamma)[fl(Z_l)]_RMS, with X used at l = m. The proof then uses [fl(Z_l)]_RMS = [Z_l]_RMS+O(epsilon), [Z_l]_RMS = sqrt(N_{l+1}...N_m)[X]_RMS, and an exact or first-order-accurate input RMS.

source_evidence.anchor: Section 6 statement on floating-point representation of input data
source_evidence.observation: The paper explicitly says that the preceding analysis assumed the input data to be exactly representable in machine precision. If fl(x) = x+delta instead, an additional input-rounding term must be added; the displayed one-dimensional estimate is ||T delta||_RMS <= sqrt(N)||delta||_RMS.

For the one-dimensional transform, the paper also interprets the computed roundoff error vector as T delta and derives a backward-style bound on the fictional input perturbation delta. It does not state a corresponding multidimensional input-perturbation formula on this page.

binders: Explicit: m is the number of dimensions; for each l = 1,...,m, N_l is the corresponding transform order, and s_l and t_l range independently over 0,...,N_l-1. [PDF p. 7 (printed p. 763), anchor: equation (4.1) index convention]

Explicit: X(s_1,...,s_m) is complex input data, Y(t_1,...,t_m) is the exact complex transform, and fl(Y) is the floating-point result of the nested multidimensional FFT. [PDF p. 7 (printed p. 763), anchor: equation (4.1); PDF p. 8 (printed p. 764), anchor: nested computation]

Inherited: each coordinate transform of order N_l uses Theorem 1's mixed-radix factorization. Renaming the radix factors to avoid collision with dimension indices, write N_l = product from r = 1 to M_l of n_{l,r}. [PDF p. 3 (printed p. 759), anchor: Theorem 1 definition of K; PDF p. 8 (printed p. 764), anchor: Theorem 2 reference to K(N_l,gamma)]

Explicit: epsilon is the machine-dependent arithmetic error constant, gamma >= 0 is the absolute trigonometric-error constant, and each theta in the operation models lies in [-1,1] and may differ between occurrences. [PDF p. 2 (printed p. 758), anchor: equations (3.1)-(3.2); PDF p. 3 (printed p. 759), anchor: absolute sine/cosine error model]
hypotheses: The multidimensional transform is computed as the nested sequence of one-dimensional floating-point FFTs fl(T_1 fl(T_2 ... fl(T_m X)...)). [PDF p. 8 (printed p. 764), anchor: nested computation preceding the telescoping decomposition]

Every coordinate FFT is governed by the one-dimensional Theorem 1 bound with its chosen mixed-radix constant K(N_l,gamma). [PDF p. 8 (printed p. 764), anchor: Theorem 2 and equation (4.3); PDF p. 3 (printed p. 759), anchor: Theorem 1]

The arithmetic and trigonometric computations satisfy the Wilkinson-style models (3.1)-(3.2) and the absolute sine/cosine model with the same displayed epsilon and gamma. [PDF p. 2 (printed p. 758), anchor: equations (3.1)-(3.2); PDF p. 3 (printed p. 759), anchor: absolute sine/cosine error model]

Standing operational assumption: the input data are exactly representable in machine precision. The proof notes that the weaker condition [fl(X)]_RMS = [X]_RMS+O(epsilon) is sufficient for its first-order conclusion. [PDF p. 9 (printed p. 765), anchor: completion of Theorem 2(a) and Section 6 input-representation statement]

The theta variables are bounded independently at each occurrence; no probabilistic independence or mean-zero roundoff hypothesis is used. [PDF p. 2 (printed p. 758), anchor: explanation following equations (3.1)-(3.2)]
conclusions: Theorem 2(a): [fl(Y)-Y]_RMS/Y_RMS <= epsilon times the sum from l = 1 to m of K(N_l,gamma), plus O(epsilon^2). [PDF p. 8 (printed p. 764), anchor: Theorem 2(a)]
Theorem 2(b): [fl(Y)-Y]_MAX/Y_RMS <= epsilon sqrt(N_1N_2...N_m) times the sum from l = 1 to m of K(N_l,gamma), plus O(epsilon^2). [PDF p. 8 (printed p. 764), anchor: Theorem 2(b)]
definitions_and_conventions: The exact transform is Y(t_1,...,t_m) = sum_{s_1=0}^{N_1-1} ... sum_{s_m=0}^{N_m-1} e(s_1t_1/N_1+...+s_mt_m/N_m)X(s_1,...,s_m), with no normalization factor. [PDF p. 7 (printed p. 763), anchor: equation (4.1)]

Equation (4.1) literally writes the kernel as e(q). Comparison with the explicitly defined one-dimensional kernel gives the inherited reading e(q) = exp(i 2 pi q), with positive sign; the multidimensional section does not separately define e. [PDF p. 7 (printed p. 763), anchor: equation (4.1); PDF p. 1 (printed p. 757), anchor: equation (1.1)]
E(t_1,...,t_m) = fl(Y(t_1,...,t_m))-Y(t_1,...,t_m). [PDF p. 8 (printed p. 764), anchor: multidimensional error definition]

[fl(Y)-Y]_RMS = ((sum_{t_1,...,t_m}|E(t_1,...,t_m)|^2)/(N_1...N_m))^(1/2), and [fl(Y)-Y]_MAX = max_{t_1,...,t_m}|E(t_1,...,t_m)|. [PDF p. 8 (printed p. 764), anchor: multidimensional RMS and maximum definitions]

The exact intermediates satisfy Z_0 = Y, Z_m = X, and Z_{l-1} = T_l Z_l, where T_l transforms coordinate s_l into t_l while retaining the remaining coordinates. [PDF p. 8 (printed p. 764), anchor: rewritten system following Theorem 2]

The expanded proof identity expresses fl(Y)-Y as the sum of each local floating-point coordinate-transform error propagated by the exact preceding operators T_1...T_{l-1}. [PDF p. 8 (printed p. 764), anchor: telescoping decomposition preceding equation (4.2)]
implicit_context: The denominator Y_RMS is the RMS value of the exact output Y, consistent with the paper's stated goal of bounding errors relative to the RMS output and with its earlier RMS convention. [PDF p. 1 (printed p. 757), anchor: abstract and introductory norm definitions; PDF p. 8 (printed p. 764), anchor: Theorem 2]

The unnormalized coordinate transform obeys [Z_{l-1}]_RMS = sqrt(N_l)[Z_l]_RMS; consequently [Y]_RMS = sqrt(N_1...N_m)[X]_RMS. [PDF p. 8 (printed p. 764), anchor: equation (4.4); PDF p. 9 (printed p. 765), anchor: propagated scaling in the proof]

Before normalization, the proof obtains [fl(Y)-Y]_RMS <= epsilon times the sum of sqrt(N_1...N_l)K(N_l,gamma)[fl(Z_l)]_RMS over the coordinate stages, with X in the final term, plus O(epsilon^2). [PDF p. 9 (printed p. 765), anchor: first displayed inequality completing Theorem 2(a)]

The K constants inherit the one-dimensional factorization and therefore depend on the selected radix decomposition and its twiddle-factor multiplications, not merely on the integer axis length in isolation. [PDF p. 2 (printed p. 758), anchor: equation (2.2); PDF p. 3 (printed p. 759), anchor: definition of K(N,gamma)]

The inherited FFT matrix factorization is stated to cover both Cooley-Tukey and Sande-Tukey variants, with different diagonal twiddle matrices. [PDF p. 2 (printed p. 758), anchor: final remark before Section 3]
statement.algorithm_linkage: Theorem 2 analyzes a product-indexed multidimensional transform implemented by applying one-dimensional FFTs along coordinates in the nested order T_m first, then T_{m-1}, and finally T_1, as shown by fl(T_1 fl(T_2 ... fl(T_m X)...)). [PDF p. 8 (printed p. 764), anchor: nested computation] Each coordinate FFT inherits Theorem 1's mixed-radix matrix factorization and K constant. [PDF p. 3 (printed p. 759), anchor: Theorem 1; PDF p. 8 (printed p. 764), anchor: equation (4.3)] The factorization applies to Cooley-Tukey and Sande-Tukey forms, with algorithm-dependent diagonal matrices. [PDF p. 2 (printed p. 758), anchor: equation (2.2) remarks]
numerical_model: For floating-point a and b, fl(a+b) = a(1+theta epsilon)+b(1+theta epsilon), with generic bounded theta values that may differ at each occurrence. [PDF p. 2 (printed p. 758), anchor: equation (3.1) and following explanation]
For floating-point a and b, fl(ab) = ab(1+theta epsilon), with |theta| <= 1. [PDF p. 2 (printed p. 758), anchor: equation (3.2) and following explanation]

With base beta, t base-beta mantissa digits, and at least t+1 digits used to accumulate sums, epsilon = 0.5 beta^(1-t) for rounded operations and beta^(1-t) for chopped operations. [PDF pp. 2-3 (printed pp. 758-759), anchor: explanation of epsilon following equation (3.2)]

If sums are accumulated with only t digits, epsilon = 0.5(1+1/beta)beta^(1-t) for rounded operations and (1+1/beta)beta^(1-t) for chopped operations. [PDF p. 3 (printed p. 759), anchor: continuation of the epsilon definition]

Trigonometric values use an absolute-error model: fl(sin(fl(a))) = sin(a)+gamma theta epsilon and fl(cos(fl(a))) = cos(a)+gamma theta epsilon; gamma is independent of input data. [PDF p. 3 (printed p. 759), anchor: absolute sine/cosine error model]
error_notions: The selected error is forward error in the computed output: computed fl(Y) minus exact Y. [PDF p. 8 (printed p. 764), anchor: definition of E]
Part (a) is an RMS forward error normalized by the exact output RMS, not by the input RMS and not coordinatewise. [PDF p. 8 (printed p. 764), anchor: Theorem 2(a)]
Part (b) is the maximum complex-magnitude forward error normalized by the exact output RMS, not by the maximum output magnitude. [PDF p. 8 (printed p. 764), anchor: Theorem 2(b)]

The conclusion is a deterministic worst-case first-order roundoff bound; no stochastic error model is invoked. [PDF p. 2 (printed p. 758), anchor: bounded generic theta model; PDF p. 8 (printed p. 764), anchor: Theorem 2]
norms: For a multidimensional array A, the paper's RMS convention is the square root of the average of |A|^2 over all N_1...N_m complex entries. [PDF p. 8 (printed p. 764), anchor: multidimensional RMS definition]
The maximum norm is the maximum complex modulus over all output multi-indices. [PDF p. 8 (printed p. 764), anchor: multidimensional maximum definition]
The exact unnormalized one-coordinate Fourier map scales RMS by sqrt(N_l): [Z_{l-1}]_RMS = sqrt(N_l)[Z_l]_RMS. [PDF p. 8 (printed p. 764), anchor: equation (4.4)]

The proof uses RMS norms of exact intermediates Z_l and computed intermediates fl(Z_l), with [fl(Z_l)]_RMS = [Z_l]_RMS+O(epsilon) for l = 1,...,m-1. [PDF p. 9 (printed p. 765), anchor: completion of Theorem 2(a)]
constants_and_indexing: For each coordinate l, using radix factors n_{l,1},...,n_{l,M_l} with N_l = product_r n_{l,r}, K(N_l,gamma) = sum_{r=1}^{M_l} alpha(n_{l,r})+(M_l-1)(3+2 gamma). This is Theorem 1's formula with factors renamed to avoid collision with multidimensional indices. [PDF p. 3 (printed p. 759), anchor: definition of K(N,gamma); PDF p. 8 (printed p. 764), anchor: Theorem 2 reference to K]
The per-radix constant is alpha(n) = sqrt(2) for n = 2, alpha(n) = 5 for n = 4, and alpha(n) = 2 sqrt(n)(n+gamma) otherwise. [PDF p. 3 (printed p. 759), anchor: piecewise definition of alpha]
For a radix-2 axis N_l = 2^M, K(2^M,gamma) = (3+sqrt(2)+2 gamma)M-(3+2 gamma). [PDF p. 3 (printed p. 759), anchor: radix-2 specialization]
For a radix-4 axis N_l = 4^M, K(4^M,gamma) = (8+2 gamma)M-(3+2 gamma). [PDF p. 3 (printed p. 759), anchor: radix-4 specialization]
The K constants include separate multiplications by the diagonal factors D_r for r = 1,...,M-1. [PDF p. 3 (printed p. 759), anchor: sentence following radix specializations]
Theorem 2 sums coordinate constants with l running exactly from 1 through m; the maximum-error conclusion has the factor sqrt(N_1N_2...N_m). [PDF p. 8 (printed p. 764), anchor: Theorem 2(a)-(b)]
higher_order_terms: Both conclusions retain an unspecified additive O(epsilon^2) term after the displayed first-order coefficient. [PDF p. 8 (printed p. 764), anchor: Theorem 2(a)-(b)]

In the one-dimensional derivation inherited by Theorem 2, the paper says O(epsilon^2) collects terms of order epsilon^2 arising from expansions of products of 1+theta epsilon factors. [PDF p. 4 (printed p. 760), anchor: expansion following equation (3.3)]

The paper does not provide an explicit constant, sign, epsilon range, or uniformity statement for the O(epsilon^2) remainder in Theorem 2. [PDF pp. 8-9 (printed pp. 764-765), anchor: Theorem 2 and completion of its proof]
exceptional_values: The paper does not discuss overflow, underflow, subnormal values, infinities, or NaNs; its operation model presumes each computed operation can be represented by equations (3.1)-(3.2). Exclusion of cases where that representation fails is therefore implicit rather than separately stated. [PDF p. 2 (printed p. 758), anchor: equations (3.1)-(3.2)]

The relative bounds divide by Y_RMS, but Theorem 2 states no explicit hypothesis Y_RMS > 0. Thus the displayed ratios are undefined for the zero transform. [PDF p. 8 (printed p. 764), anchor: Theorem 2(a)-(b)]

Input values not exactly representable in machine precision fall outside the stated operational scope and require an additional input-rounding term. The paper displays such a term only for the one-dimensional transform, not a multidimensional analogue. [PDF p. 9 (printed p. 765), anchor: Section 6 input-representation statement; PDF p. 12 (printed p. 768), anchor: continuation of input-data discussion]

undebatable_constraints: The transform is the unnormalized product-indexed complex Fourier transform with positive exponential sign and indices 0 through N_l-1 in every coordinate. [PDF p. 7 (printed p. 763), anchor: equation (4.1); PDF p. 1 (printed p. 757), anchor: equation (1.1)]
The computation is a nested sequence of m one-dimensional floating-point FFTs, not a direct multidimensional summation. [PDF p. 8 (printed p. 764), anchor: nested computation]
Theorem 2(a) has coefficient sum_{l=1}^m K(N_l,gamma), with no factor sqrt(N_1...N_m) in the relative RMS bound. [PDF p. 8 (printed p. 764), anchor: Theorem 2(a)]
Theorem 2(b) has the additional factor sqrt(N_1...N_m) and still normalizes by Y_RMS. [PDF p. 8 (printed p. 764), anchor: Theorem 2(b)]

Each K(N_l,gamma) is the factorization-dependent mixed-radix constant from Theorem 1, including its piecewise alpha values and the (M_l-1)(3+2 gamma) term. [PDF p. 3 (printed p. 759), anchor: definition of K(N,gamma)]
The error is measured using complex magnitudes and RMS averaging over exactly N_1...N_m output entries. [PDF p. 8 (printed p. 764), anchor: multidimensional RMS definition]

The first-order proof depends on exact scaling by sqrt(N_l) at each unnormalized coordinate transform and on propagation of every local coordinate-transform error. [PDF pp. 8-9 (printed pp. 764-765), anchor: equations (4.2)-(4.4) and proof completion]
The displayed result is first-order in epsilon and retains, rather than discards, an O(epsilon^2) remainder. [PDF p. 8 (printed p. 764), anchor: Theorem 2(a)-(b)]

The preceding analysis assumes exactly representable input data; input rounding is not included in Theorem 2's displayed coefficient. [PDF p. 9 (printed p. 765), anchor: Section 6 input-representation statement]

ambiguities.issue: The multidimensional section uses e(q) for the Fourier kernel without explicitly defining that notation. [PDF p. 7 (printed p. 763), anchor: equation (4.1)]
ambiguities.evidence: The earlier one-dimensional transform explicitly uses exp(i 2 pi jk/N), so e(q) = exp(i 2 pi q) is strongly indicated but inherited rather than stated locally. [PDF p. 1 (printed p. 757), anchor: equation (1.1); PDF p. 7 (printed p. 763), anchor: equation (4.1)]
ambiguities.impact: A formal transcription should either preserve e as an abstract kernel tied to equation (1.1), or document that the identification e(q) = exp(i 2 pi q) is inferred from the paper's earlier convention. [PDF pp. 1 and 7, anchors: equations (1.1) and (4.1)]

ambiguities.issue: Theorem 2 divides by Y_RMS but does not explicitly require Y_RMS to be nonzero. [PDF p. 8 (printed p. 764), anchor: Theorem 2(a)-(b)]
ambiguities.evidence: Both displayed conclusions contain Y_RMS in the denominator, and no nonzero-output clause accompanies the theorem. [PDF p. 8 (printed p. 764), anchor: Theorem 2 statement]
ambiguities.impact: The relative form is meaningful only for Y_RMS > 0; the zero-input and zero-output case requires a separate absolute formulation or an added nonzero hypothesis. [PDF p. 8 (printed p. 764), anchor: Theorem 2]

ambiguities.issue: Gamma is described as depending on how trigonometric values are computed for a transform of a given order, while Theorem 2 uses one common gamma for all coordinate orders. [PDF p. 3 (printed p. 759), anchor: absolute sine/cosine error model; PDF p. 8 (printed p. 764), anchor: Theorem 2]
ambiguities.evidence: The paper does not state whether the multidimensional gamma is identical for every axis or is a common upper bound on order-dependent constants. [PDF pp. 3 and 8, anchors: gamma definition and Theorem 2]
ambiguities.impact: A faithful formalization should use the theorem's single common gamma; replacing it by separate gamma_l values would be a generalization unless a common maximum is explicitly introduced. [PDF p. 8 (printed p. 764), anchor: sum of K(N_l,gamma)]

ambiguities.issue: The O(epsilon^2) remainder is not quantified beyond its asymptotic order. [PDF pp. 8-9 (printed pp. 764-765), anchor: Theorem 2 and proof completion]
ambiguities.evidence: No remainder constant, dependence on dimensions, radix factors, gamma, or input, and no valid epsilon interval are supplied. [PDF pp. 4 and 8-9, anchors: explanation of O(epsilon^2) and Theorem 2]
ambiguities.impact: The source supports a first-order asymptotic inequality, not an explicit finite-epsilon bound obtained by simply deleting the remainder. [PDF p. 8 (printed p. 764), anchor: Theorem 2]

ambiguities.issue: The theorem statement itself does not mention input representation, while the proof needs an exact or first-order-accurate input RMS and Section 6 says exact representability was assumed. [PDF p. 9 (printed p. 765), anchor: completion of Theorem 2(a) and input-representation statement]
ambiguities.evidence: The proof allows [fl(X)]_RMS = [X]_RMS+O(epsilon), but the later scope statement describes the preceding analysis as assuming exact machine representability. [PDF p. 9 (printed p. 765), anchor: proof completion and Section 6]
ambiguities.impact: The conservative source contract should retain exact representability as the standing assumption; using only the weaker RMS condition must be identified as a proof-level relaxation. [PDF p. 9 (printed p. 765), anchor: relevant assumptions]

ambiguities.issue: The paper gives no explicit exceptional-value policy for overflow, underflow, or nonfinite arithmetic. [PDF p. 2 (printed p. 758), anchor: equations (3.1)-(3.2)]
ambiguities.evidence: Only multiplicative/additive relative-error representations for ordinary floating-point operands are specified. [PDF p. 2 (printed p. 758), anchor: Wilkinson models]
ambiguities.impact: Any formal model excluding exceptional values is an implicit operational precondition needed to make the displayed arithmetic equations applicable, rather than a separately stated theorem hypothesis. [PDF p. 2 (printed p. 758), anchor: equations (3.1)-(3.2)]

contract_plain_english: For an m-dimensional unnormalized complex Fourier transform, compute the output by nesting one-dimensional floating-point FFTs along the m coordinates, with each coordinate FFT using its own mixed-radix factorization and the corresponding Theorem 1 constant K(N_l,gamma). [PDF pp. 7-8 (printed pp. 763-764), anchors: equation (4.1), nested computation, and Theorem 2] Under the paper's deterministic Wilkinson arithmetic model, its absolute trigonometric-error model, and its standing assumption of exactly representable input data, the output RMS forward error divided by the exact output RMS is at most epsilon sum_l K(N_l,gamma)+O(epsilon^2). [PDF pp. 2-3 and 8-9 (printed pp. 758-759 and 764-765), anchors: numerical models, Theorem 2(a), and input-representation scope] The theorem's second part bounds maximum output error divided by the same output RMS by epsilon sqrt(N_1...N_m) sum_l K(N_l,gamma)+O(epsilon^2). [PDF p. 8 (printed p. 764), anchor: Theorem 2(b)] The result is asymptotic, factorization-dependent, and meaningful in its relative form only when the exact output RMS is nonzero. [PDF pp. 3 and 8 (printed pp. 759 and 764), anchors: definition of K and Theorem 2]
